# Colour and style

::: {.doc-lead}
Choose a theme, keep colours consistent, and define scales that travel with the plot.
:::

## Start with a theme

Use `fp.use_light()` for a white publication background, `fp.use_paper()` for warm paper, or `fp.use_dark()` for a dark background. Call it before creating the figure. These change Matplotlib's style settings; existing artists keep their values.

## Colormap and palette collections

Use a **colormap** for numerical values and a **palette** for named categories. Map names are registered with Matplotlib when you import fluxplot, together with their reversed `_r` forms.

```python
import fluxplot as fp

fp.use_paper()
# These names work in cmap= on fluxplot and Matplotlib calls.
sequential = fp.colors.maps.get("crameri.batlow")
diverging = fp.colors.maps.get("tol.sunset")
category_colours = fp.colors.palettes.get("tol", "bright")
```

| Collection | Maps | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `flexoki` | 5 | Flux's house maps and colour ramps |
| `mpl` | 86 | Matplotlib's built-in colormaps, in its documented groups |
| `crameri` | 60 | Fabio Crameri's Scientific colour maps |
| `tol` | 20 | Paul Tol's continuous and discrete maps, plus his categorical palettes |
| `cmasher` | 57 | CMasher colormaps |
| `brewer` | palettes | ColorBrewer sets: 9-class sequential, 11-class diverging and the qualitative sets |

`fp.colors.maps.names("crameri")` lists a collection, and `fp.colors.maps.info("tol.sunset")` describes a map. `fp.colors.maps.truncate("batlow", 0.2, 0.8)` selects part of a map, and `fp.colors.maps.discretize("viridis", [0, 2, 5, 10])` returns a colormap and normalization for bins.

Every `fp.use_*` theme installs `cmasher.rainforest` (`fp.style.SEQUENTIAL`) as Matplotlib's default `image.cmap`, so a heatmap without `cmap=` is in the house style; `fp.style.DEFAULT_DIVERGING` names the diverging default. You can override either for any plot with `cmap=`. In a signature plot's `palette=`, a colour name such as `"red"` selects a pale-to-deep ramp of that one hue, while `"flexoki.red"` selects the 13-step Flexoki ramp.

<details><summary>Map details, derived maps and where the definitions live</summary>

**Map information.** `fp.colors.maps.info(name)` reports a map's type (`sequential`, `diverging`,
`cyclic`, `qualitative` or `misc`), its family, its table size `N`, whether it is `discrete` (a
listed map of at most `fp.colors.DISCRETE_MAX` = 32 colours, a set of classes to pick from), and
whether it is perceptually `uniform` (`True`, `False`, or `None` when not assessed). Each
definition's `colors` is the map's exact lookup table, so a consumer reproduces it colour for
colour. `fp.colors.maps.get("batlow")` also resolves a bare name, searching the collections in
the order of the table above.

**House maps.** The `flexoki` collection holds `flexoki.sequential`, `.warm`, `.diverging`,
`.terrain` and `.spectrum`. They are linear ramps through palette anchors
(`fp.colors.FLEXOKI_MAP_ANCHORS`) and therefore *not* perceptually uniform
(`info()["uniform"] is False`). Their older bare names, such as `flexoki_diverging`, are aliases
of the same tables.

**Derived maps.** `truncate` returns the stretch of a map as a map of its own, named like
`crameri.batlow[0.2:0.8]`, a name that `fp.colors.maps.get` (and therefore a recipe) resolves
again. `discretize(..., extend="both")` returns a `(ListedColormap, BoundaryNorm)` pair with one
colour per bin, which any helper accepts as `cmap=` / `norm=`; the colour scale is then recorded
as `kind: "binned"`.

**Palettes.** `fp.colors.palettes` holds `flexoki` (the default), `brewer` and `tol`.
`fp.colors.palettes.brewer["Blues"]` and `fp.colors.palettes.get("tol", "bright")` return lists
of hex strings.

**Definitions.** Every colormap and palette is plain data in the package
(`src/fluxplot/definitions/colormaps.json` and `palettes.json`), so nothing beyond Matplotlib is
imported at runtime, and Flux bundles the same files for its pickers. The JSON is generated by
`tools/build_color_definitions.py` from the upstream packages (matplotlib, cmcrameri, tol-colors,
cmasher); it is a build-time step, re-run only to refresh a collection
(`uv run --with cmcrameri --with tol-colors python tools/build_color_definitions.py`; a collection
whose package is missing keeps its shipped definition). The Flexoki palette has one canonical
source, the design-token export `src/fluxplot/definitions/flexoki.tokens.json`: `fp.colors.flex`
and the `flexoki` palette collection are both built from it. fluxplot's "green" is the tokens'
custom `GRN` hue; Flexoki's original green is `olive`.

</details>

## Theme metadata {#themes-a-consumer-can-follow}

The manifest records the theme in force at save time:

```jsonc
// "theme" is "light", "dark", "paper", …; null once an rcParam was changed by hand.
"style": {"theme": "light",
          "tokens": {"ink": "#…", "label": "#…", "tick": "#…", "axis": "#…",
                     "grid": "#…", "plot": "#…", "paper": "#…"}}
```

The tokens are the scaffold colours by role, as lowercase hex. Every scaffold element painted
with one of them carries `data-ink-fill` or `data-ink-stroke` naming the token:

| Element | Token |
|---|---|
| tick labels and titles | `ink` |
| axis titles | `label` |
| ticks | `tick` |
| spines | `axis` |
| gridlines | `grid` |
| the axes background (`axes.background`) | `plot` |
| the figure background (`figure.background`) | `paper` |

Overlays that a helper drew in the theme's ink, such as a significance bracket, are tagged too.
Data colours are never tagged, so Flux can restyle a light plot's furniture for a dark deck and
leave the science alone.

`fp.save(..., theme_vars=True)` additionally rewrites those paints as `var(--fx-<token>, <hex>)`
for a CSS-aware host. It is off by default: browsers and rsvg honour the fallback, but Illustrator
and Inkscape have not yet been checked. A rerun with
`FLUX_PARAMS={"__fluxplot__": {"theme": "dark"}}` makes every `fp.use_*` call apply that theme,
and the recipe records the theme in force under `__fluxplot__.theme`.

## Consistent category colours {#series-colours-and-the-same-colour-for-the-same-thing-everywhere}

Every series records its primary paint in the manifest, as `series[].color`:

```jsonc
"color": {"hex": "#35ab49", "alpha": 1.0, "token": "flexoki.green-400",
          "palette": {"name": "flexoki.light", "index": 2}}
```

`token` is the exact palette token when one names the colour, and `palette` gives its slot in
the active cycle when it came from there. A colour-mapped collection records `"varies"`, and its
`scale` names the colour scale. The glowbar and fluxbox payloads record the `palette` each
category's shades came from.

`fp.colors.categories` keeps category colours consistent across figures:

```python
# Pin a colour:
fp.colors.categories.assign({"SD": "#bc5215"})
# The pinned colour, or the next unused palette slot:
colour = fp.colors.categories.get("sleep")
# Write the pinned colours to the project file:
fp.colors.categories.save()
```

`get()` returns the colour pinned to a category; otherwise it assigns the next unused slot of the
palette (by default the theme's cycle) in first-request order and remembers it. A category
therefore keeps its colour whether or not the others are on the plot. Surface maps
(`categorical_colors`), glowbar and fluxbox group colours, and `tag_seaborn`'s hue levels all
consult it.

`save()` and `load()` write and read the pinned colours in the project file `fluxplot.colors.json`
(`{"spec": "fluxplot/colors", "version": 1, "categories": {"SD": "#bc5215"}, "palette": "flexoki"}`).
The first use loads it automatically from `$FLUXPLOT_COLORS`, or from the nearest such file
between the working directory and the Git root; nothing is ever written implicitly. Setting
`categories.auto_series = True` colours `fp.line` and `fp.scatter` series by their name when the
call gives no colour (off by default).

Two recipe controls apply on a rerun: `__fluxplot__.palette = "tol.bright"` makes every
`fp.use_*` install that palette as the colour cycle (glowbar categories draw from it too), and
`__fluxplot__.series = {"<series id>": {"color": "#…"}}` recolours a series. The helpers and the
signature plots check both before drawing.

## Signature plots on dark grounds

The glowbar, fluxbox and hexmatrix judge every ink against the ground they are drawn on. On a
dark theme:

- point rims lighten instead of darkening, and the shades stay at least 20 lightness units above
  the ground;
- the mean and median inks lift off their marks instead of deepening;
- connectors take the theme's grid neutral, and a qualitative palette's group ink is the light
  neutral;
- a hexmatrix's single-colour ramp turns around, running from deep near the ground to pale at the
  top. It is named `hexmatrix.mono-dark:#…`, so a rerun rebuilds it.

fluxplot's test suite checks a WCAG contrast of at least 1.5 for every mark, and at least 3 for
bracket and identity lines, under the light, paper and dark themes.

## Value × confidence {#value-and-confidence}

A colour-mapped mark can carry a second, opacity channel: `alpha_by=` on `fp.hexmatrix`
(`"count"`, a column, a per-point or per-hexagon array, or a matrix in matrix mode), `fp.heatmap`
(a matrix of the same shape — p-values, n) and `fp.scatter` (one value per point), with
`alpha_range=(0.25, 1.0)` and `alpha_norm="linear"|"log"`. Each element's alpha runs over the
range with its value (a missing value takes the low end), set as per-element alpha so matplotlib
renders it; the manifest records the channel as `colorScales[].alpha = {source, range, norm}` and
every element carries `data-alpha-value`, so a consumer can recompute `fill-opacity` live.

For example, use observation counts as `alpha_by` to make sparsely sampled regions lighter.
Higher channel values receive higher opacity, so transform an uncertainty measure explicitly if
lower values should be more prominent.

## Accessibility lint

`fp.colorcheck` asks what a plot's colours do for the reader:

- `simulate(colors, "deuteranomaly")` applies the Machado (2009) colour-vision-deficiency
  matrices for protanomaly, deuteranomaly or tritanomaly, at every published severity.
- `greyscale` shows the black-and-white print; `delta_e` is CIEDE2000 and `contrast` the WCAG 2
  ratio.
- `check_palette(colors, bg, text=…)` finds pairs that collapse under a deficiency
  (`cvd-confusable`, ΔE < 10) or in greyscale (`greyscale-confusable`, ΔL\* < 10), and marks
  (`low-contrast-mark`, < 3:1) or text (`low-contrast-text`, < 4.5:1) too faint against the
  ground.
- `check_colormap` flags a map whose ΔE steps vary too much (`non-uniform`) or a sequential map
  whose lightness reverses (`non-monotone`).

`fp.save(..., lint="warn")` runs `check_figure` on the tagged series and text inks. Findings go
to `SaveResult.warnings` and the manifest's `quality.color`; `lint="error"` refuses the save.
Linting is off by default.

The house colour cycles are ordered so that no two *adjacent* colours collapse for a
colour-deficient reader: `fp.CYCLE_ORDER` is blue, orange, purple, green, magenta, yellow, cyan,
red. The smallest adjacent distance under any deficiency is ΔE 20 in the light cycle and 15 in
the dark one. This order was introduced on 30 September 2026 (cyan used to sit next to magenta,
at ΔE 5.6), so plots that let the cycle pick their colours changed from the third series on when
regenerated. Order alone cannot guarantee greyscale separation; vary the marker or line style
for a figure that must print in black and white.

## Colour controls in the recipe

Every colour scale is a recipe control: `fp.save` writes its complete state under
`recipe.params.__fluxplot__[<key>]`, and Flux's **Colour scales** editor edits it and regenerates
the plot. A control has this shape (`|` separates the alternatives):

```jsonc
{"cmap": "magma" | {"lut": ["#…"], "under": "#…", "over": "#…", "bad": "#…"},
 "reversed": false,
 "vmin": 1, "vmax": 50,
 "norm": {"kind": "linear" | "log" | "symlog" | "power" | "twoslope" | "centered",
          "vcenter": 0, "gamma": 0.5, "linthresh": 1, "linscale": 1},
 "extend": "neither" | "min" | "max" | "both"}
```

The helpers read the controls from `FLUX_PARAMS` automatically. A control that merely restates
what the script asked for (the replay of a recorded save) keeps the script's own objects — a
`ListedColormap` with no resolvable name included — so regeneration never fails on its own
output; a control that differs is applied, and an impossible one (an unknown map, a log norm with
`vmin <= 0`, a twoslope centre outside the limits) raises a `ValueError` naming the key.
`extend` reaches the colour key drawn with `fp.colorbar`. The old flat `{cmap, vmin, vmax}` is
still understood.

The key names the **series** (`rates`), never the axes' position, so adding a subplot cannot
orphan an edit. A second colour-mapped series with the same name gets `panel.<name>.rates` or
`axes.<n>.rates`, and `key=` names it explicitly. Controls saved by an older Flux under the
positional key are still honoured. Other recipe options are described in
[Recipes and parameters](/docs/save-and-recipes.html#recipes-and-parameters).

## Share a scale across panels

Use `fp.color_scale` to give multiple plots a common range and colour map. The [matrices and colour scales guide](/docs/matrices-and-scales.html#shared-scales) gives the pattern and explains how limits are combined.
